\chapter{La Casa Por Fuera}
\label{ch:es-casa-fuera}
\hlchaptermodality{444}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report what is wrong with a home and say what I did about it: the heating, the material, the garden, the thing I covered, the trolley I took to the shop.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la calefacción]{la calefacción — heat, made}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-calefaccion}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el calor} and \textbf{el frío}. It is January and the flat is cold. Name the thing that is not working.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la calefacción}
\textbf{la calefacción} — the heating.

\emph{No funciona la calefacción} — the heating is not working, which is the sentence a tenant needs first. \emph{Calefacción central} — central heating. \emph{Poner la calefacción} — to put the heating on.

\begin{cousinweb}
Two pieces, and you own both.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{where you have it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{cale-} & \emph{calor}, heat \\
\textbf{-facción} & \emph{facere}, to make \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Heat-making.} The second half is the same \emph{facere} that sits under \emph{hacer} and under \textbf{la factura}, which you met as \emph{a making}. A \emph{factura} is a making of accounts; a \emph{calefacción} is a making of heat.

English has the pieces too, in \textbf{calorie} — a unit of heat — and in the \textbf{-faction} of \emph{satisfaction} and \emph{liquefaction}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Notice that Spanish names the \emph{process}, not the \emph{device}.

English \textbf{heating} can mean the radiators, the boiler, or the service. Spanish \textbf{calefacción} is the making-of-heat, and the hardware has its own words — \emph{el radiador}, \emph{la caldera}. That is why the bill says \emph{calefacción} and the plumber talks about \emph{la caldera}: the two are not the same noun.

So \emph{la factura de la calefacción} is the bill for heat-made, not the bill for a machine. Both words on that line come from \emph{facere}, one making heat and one making the account of it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la calefacción}
  \item the heating is not working and I am cold
  \item what the two pieces of the word mean
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The heating? (\textbf{La calefacción}.) What does the second half mean? (\textbf{To make}.) Which other word you have is built on it? (\emph{\textbf{La factura}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la madera]{la madera — the stuff a tree is for}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-madera}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la mesa}, \textbf{la silla} and \textbf{el árbol}. Two of those are made of the third. Name what they are made of.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la madera}
\textbf{la madera} — wood, as a material.

\emph{Una mesa de madera} — a wooden table. Spanish says \textbf{de madera}, of wood, where English turns the noun into an adjective.

The tree is \emph{el árbol}, the wood you build with is \emph{la madera}, and a wood you walk in is \emph{el bosque} — three words where English stretches one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{madera} is Latin \textbf{māteria}, and \emph{māteria} meant \textbf{timber} before it meant anything else.

Behind it sits \textbf{māter}, mother. A tree's \emph{māteria} was its trunk — the part that puts out the branches, the mothering stock. Only later did Roman philosophers borrow the word for \emph{the stuff a thing is made of} in general.

So the abstract sense came \textbf{second}. Matter was named after wood, not the other way round.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
That one Latin word reached Spanish \textbf{twice}, and this is the third pair of its kind you have met.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{the road it took} \\
\midrule
\textbf{la madera} & carried in every mouth, worn down \\
\textbf{la materia} & lifted off the page by scholars \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Māteria} spoken for a thousand years became \textbf{madera} and kept the concrete sense: the planks. \emph{Māteria} read off the page centuries later came back as \textbf{la materia} and kept the abstract one: matter, subject-matter, a school subject.

You have seen the shape before — \textbf{nadar} beside \textbf{la natación}, \textbf{hacer} beside \textbf{la factura}, and now \textbf{madera} beside \textbf{materia}. The worn twin is the everyday one; the learned twin is the one on the timetable, the bill or the syllabus. When two Spanish words look loosely alike and one is plainer than the other, this is the first thing to suspect.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la madera}
  \item a wooden table and a wooden chair
  \item why \emph{madera} and \emph{materia} are the same word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Wood? (\textbf{La madera}.) A wooden table? (\textbf{Una mesa de madera}.) What did \emph{māteria} mean first? (\textbf{Timber}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[plantar]{plantar — pressed in with the foot}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-plantar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la planta}, \textbf{el jardín} and \textbf{la tierra}. You have the thing, the place and the ground. Name the act.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: plantar}
\textbf{plantar} — to plant.

\emph{Plantamos un árbol en el jardín} — we planted a tree in the garden. \emph{Plantar cara} is to stand up to somebody, and \emph{dejar plantado} is to stand somebody up — to leave them planted where they were waiting.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la planta} has three meanings in Spanish and one origin.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the sense} & \textbf{what it names} \\
\midrule
la planta del pie & the \textbf{sole} of the foot \\
una planta & a growing plant \\
la primera planta & a storey of a building \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin \textbf{planta} was the sole of the foot, and nothing else. To \emph{plantāre} was to \textbf{press a cutting into the soil with your heel} — the actual gesture a Roman gardener made. The plant is named after the foot that put it there.

The storey follows the same foot: a \emph{planta} of a building is a \textbf{floor plan}, the outline you would leave standing on it, which is why English \textbf{plan} is the same word again.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This is worth holding next to \textbf{madera}.

\emph{Madera} went the other way: a concrete thing (timber) whose name was borrowed upward into an abstraction (matter). \emph{Planta} started as a body part and spread sideways into two unrelated-looking objects — a shrub and a floor of a building.

Neither is a word splitting into homonyms by accident. Both are \textbf{one image being reused}, and if you can recover the image you get the whole family instead of three separate entries. For \emph{planta}, the image is a foot pressing down.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{plantar}
  \item we planted a tree in the garden
  \item the three meanings of \emph{planta}, and the one picture behind them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To plant? (\textbf{Plantar}.) What did Latin \emph{planta} mean? (\textbf{The sole of the foot}.) What is \emph{la primera planta}? (\textbf{The first floor}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cubrir]{cubrir — and the lid that comes off again}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-cubrir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{abrir} and \textbf{cerrado}. Say \textbf{plantar}. You have put a cutting in the ground and the frost is coming. Name what you do to it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cubrir}
\textbf{cubrir} — to cover.

\emph{Cubre la olla} — cover the pot. \emph{El seguro no lo cubre} — the insurance does not cover it, which is the sense you will meet on paper rather than in a kitchen. \textbf{el cubierto} is a place setting at table, the knife and fork laid out — what \emph{covers} your place.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a third irregular participle}]
\textbf{abrir} gave you \textbf{abierto} and \textbf{cerrar} gave you \textbf{cerrado}. \emph{Cubrir} follows \emph{abrir}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{participle} \\
\midrule
cerrar & cerrado — regular \\
abrir & \textbf{abierto} — irregular \\
cubrir & \textbf{cubierto} — irregular \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Abrir} and \emph{cubrir} both end in \textbf{-brir}, and both break the same way. That is not a coincidence you have to memorise separately: the handful of irregular participles come in small families, and finding one member gives you the others. \emph{Descubrir} makes \textbf{descubierto}, because it is \emph{cubrir} with something on the front.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{cooperīre} — \textbf{co-} together, plus \textbf{operīre}, to shut or cover over. \emph{Operīre} is itself \textbf{ob-} plus a root meaning \emph{to close}, and its opposite, \textbf{aperīre}, gave you \textbf{abrir}. So \emph{cubrir} and \emph{abrir} are not merely alike in shape; they are two halves of one Latin pair.

And now the prefix that earns its keep:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what des- does} \\
\midrule
cubrir & put the cover on \\
\textbf{descubrir} & \textbf{take it off — to discover} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Descansar} taught you \emph{des-} as an undoing, and this is the same job done plainly: to \emph{discover} something is to \textbf{uncover} it. Compare \emph{disfrutar}, where the prefix did not reverse at all. Same shape, two behaviours, and only the meaning of the whole word tells you which you have.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cubrir}, then \emph{cubierto}
  \item cover the pot, the frost is coming
  \item \emph{descubrir}, and what \emph{des-} is doing to it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To cover? (\textbf{Cubrir}.) The participle? (\textbf{Cubierto} — irregular, like \emph{abierto}.) To discover? (\textbf{Descubrir} — to un-cover.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el carrito]{el carrito — a small cart, and a very large ending}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-carrito}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el supermercado} and \textbf{el coche}. Say \textbf{cubrir}. You are at the door of the shop with a week's shopping to do. Name what you take.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el carrito}
\textbf{el carrito} — the trolley, the cart.

\emph{El carrito de la compra} — the shopping trolley. \emph{Un carrito de bebé} — a pushchair. On a website, \emph{añadir al carrito} is \textbf{add to basket}, and that is where you will meet the word most often.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{carro} plus \textbf{-ito}.

\emph{El carro} is a cart, from Latin \textbf{carrus}, a wagon — a word Latin itself took from Gaulish, and the same one behind English \textbf{car}, \textbf{carry} and \textbf{cargo}. Add \textbf{-ito} and you have a small one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that does more than shrink}]
\textbf{-ito} and \textbf{-ita} attach to almost any noun, and size is only its first job.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{with -ito} & \textbf{what it adds} \\
\midrule
un momento & un moment\textbf{ito} & \emph{a moment} $\to$ \emph{one moment, please} \\
ahora & ahor\textbf{ita} & now $\to$ right now, or soon \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Momentito} is not a shorter moment. The ending softens the request, the way English softens one by adding \emph{a little} or \emph{if you would}. Spanish speakers use it constantly for that, not for measuring.

Two things to watch. \textbf{Spelling follows sound}: \emph{poco} becomes \emph{poquito}, because \emph{c} before \emph{i} would go soft and the word must keep its \textbf{k}. And the ending has a cousin, \textbf{-illo}, which shrinks less kindly — \emph{un librillo} is faintly dismissive where \emph{un librito} is affectionate.

So when a Spanish speaker adds \emph{-ito} to something that is not small, they are usually being warm rather than inaccurate.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el carrito}
  \item add it to the basket
  \item \emph{un momentito}, and what the ending is doing there
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The trolley? (\textbf{El carrito}.) What does \textbf{-ito} add besides size? (\textbf{Warmth, or softening}.) Why is it \emph{poquito} and not \emph{pocito}? (\textbf{To keep the hard k}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(calefacción, madera, plantar, cubrir …]{(calefacción, madera, plantar, cubrir, carrito) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R444-repaso-casa}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{the heating}, \emph{wood}, \emph{to plant}, \emph{to cover}, \emph{the trolley}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three things a word can do on its way into Spanish}]
Every word in this chapter came from Latin, and no two arrived the same way.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what happened to it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{madera} & arrived \textbf{twice} — and \emph{materia} is the other one \\
\textbf{planta} & arrived once and \textbf{spread} into three meanings \\
\textbf{carrito} & arrived, then Spanish \textbf{built on it} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Madera} and \emph{materia} are one word on two roads, the worn twin and the learned twin. \emph{Planta} is one road and one word that kept being reused — sole of the foot, then the cutting pressed in by it, then the floor plan you stand on. \emph{Carrito} is neither: \emph{carro} came in, and the \textbf{-ito} on the end is Spanish's own work, added centuries after Latin had finished.

Those three cover most of what you will meet. A word arrives twice, or it arrives once and stretches, or it arrives and the language grows something new on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the heating is not working
  \item cover the pot before the frost
  \item a wooden table, and why \emph{madera} and \emph{materia} are one word
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now report what is wrong with a home and say what you did about it} — the heating, the material, the garden, the thing you covered, the trolley you took to the shop. Between this and the contract chapter you can hold up most of a tenancy in Spanish.

You also have a third irregular participle. \textbf{Cubierto} joins \textbf{abierto}, and they break together because they rhyme: the irregulars come in small families, so finding one gives you the rest.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The participle of \emph{cubrir}? (\textbf{Cubierto}.) Wood? (\textbf{La madera}.) The heating? (\textbf{La calefacción}.) Which of those three is a doublet? (\emph{\textbf{Madera}}, with \emph{materia}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un aviso del casero) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C444-sintesis-casa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la calefacción} and \emph{cubrir}. The notice you are about to read uses one of them, and the reply uses the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — un aviso en el portal}

\begin{quote}
Se informa a los vecinos de que la \textbf{calefacción} quedará apagada el martes por trabajos en la caldera. Los suelos de \textbf{madera} del portal se barnizarán el mismo día. Rogamos no pisar.
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — un mensaje al casero}

\begin{quote}
Buenos días. La ventana del salón no cierra bien y entra frío. También he \textbf{plantado} las macetas que dejó en la terraza, pero habrá que \textbf{cubrirlas} si hiela. ¿Puede pasar el técnico esta semana?
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item what will be off on Tuesday, and why
  \item what the residents are asked not to do
  \item the two things the tenant reports, and the one request
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Look at \textbf{cubrirlas} in the second message.

The pronoun is stuck on the \textbf{end} of the infinitive: \emph{cubrir} plus \emph{las}, the flowerpots. Spanish attaches the object to an infinitive rather than putting it in front, and does the same to a command — \emph{cúbrelas} — and to a gerund. English never does this, which is why \emph{habrá que cubrirlas} looks like one long word and is two.

The first notice will not do that, because it has no people in it: \emph{se informa}, \emph{se barnizarán}, \emph{rogamos}. It is the impersonal register you met on the council's page, and the contrast between the two texts is the whole point of reading them together. A neighbour writes with pronouns; a notice writes without.

Even the \textbf{-ito} ending belongs to the message and not the notice. Nobody puts \emph{un momentito} on a formal sign.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Five sentences to a landlord: say the heating is not working, say which room, say what you planted, say you had to cover it, and ask for someone to come.

Then check yourself: did you write \textbf{cubrirlas} as one word?
\end{tcolorbox}
